supplements.heading: EBT card / balance problems — not a policy question
supplements.text: EBT card issues (lost or stolen card, PIN reset, balance, transaction disputes, skimming/stolen benefits) are handled by EBT Customer Service, not by a policy citation. California EBT Customer Service: 1-888-328-2656 (24/7) — advise the client to call immediately to freeze a lost/stolen card. THE OFFICIAL self-service tools are the ebtEDGE mobile app and the ebtEDGE web portal (and California's cardholder site www.ebt.ca.gov) — use these or EBT Customer Service to check a balance, set or change a PIN, and freeze a lost or stolen card. Do card-security actions (PIN changes, freezing a card) through the official ebtEDGE app/portal or Customer Service, NOT a third-party balance app: per CDSS's FFY2024 EBT management-evaluation response, secure PIN changes are made 'by calling EBT Customer Service or by enrolling in the ebtEDGE mobile application and web portal.' The general benefit-issuance rules are at 7 CFR 274. STOLEN / skimmed benefits: California does NOT require a police report to request replacement of electronically stolen benefits (confirmed in FNS's FFY2024 EBT management evaluation of CDSS) — do not tell a client to file a police report first. The replacement rules and claim window have shifted recently, so confirm the current CDSS process and deadline, but never gate the ask on a police report.

supplements.heading: What SNAP can / cannot buy
supplements.text: SNAP buys staple grocery food: fruits, vegetables, meat, dairy, bread, cereals, snacks, and seeds/plants that produce food. It CANNOT buy: hot foods or foods prepared for immediate consumption at the point of sale, alcohol, tobacco, vitamins/medicines/supplements, or any nonfood household goods (soap, paper products, pet food, hygiene items). The governing definition is 7 CFR 271.2 ("eligible food"). Exception: the Restaurant Meals Program (statewide in California per AB 942) lets certain elderly, disabled, or homeless recipients buy prepared meals at participating restaurants. Confirm current CDSS RMP details.

supplements.citation: 7 CFR 273.24 (ABAWD) — CURRENT rules per H.R.1 / OBBBA §10102 (Pub. L. 119-21); CDSS ACL 25-93; ACL 25-34 (CF 887 / CF 888 forms)
supplements.heading: ABAWD time limit — CURRENT rules (post-OBBBA), California
supplements.text: The ABAWD time limit (3 countable months of SNAP in a 36-month period unless meeting the work rule) now applies to adults 18 through 64. Age edges differ BY STATE: in California a person is no longer an ABAWD the first of the month after their 65th birthday; Texas ends it the month the person turns 65 — do not state one nationally. Work rule: 80 hours/month (~20/week) of work, approved E&T, community service/volunteering, or workfare. WORKFARE HOURS = the household's monthly allotment ÷ the HIGHEST applicable minimum wage (state, county, or city), rounded DOWN, and workfare is NOT combinable with other qualifying activities. Note stand-alone E&T job search / job club is a NON-qualifying activity (countable only up to 9 hours), so 'approved E&T' does not automatically satisfy the 80 hours. CURRENT ABAWD time-limit exemptions and how to verify each: (1) exempt from work registration [MPP 63-407] — no separate proof; (2) under 18 or over 64 — date of birth; (3) physically or mentally unfit — receipt of or pending application for a disability benefit (SSI/SSDI/VA/workers' comp); OR 'obviously unfit', which is determined by the worker at interview and needs only detailed case notes; OR, for non-obvious unfitness, form CF 887 or a WRITTEN OR VERBAL statement from a medical or mental-health professional (physicians, nurse practitioners, dentists, social workers). IMPORTANT: homelessness, drug/alcohol addiction, and domestic violence are now only INDICATORS of possible unfitness — they must be tied to physical/mental unfitness, they are not exemptions in themselves; (4) responsible for a dependent CHILD UNDER 14 (narrowed by OBBBA from under 18; the child must be in the same SNAP household) — DO NOT confuse this with the CF 886 'good cause' for missing work hours, which is a lack of childcare for a child under 12: two different age cutoffs (14 vs 12) for two different purposes; (5) pregnant — client statement is sufficient; (6) participating at least half-time in an Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR) training program; (7) an Indian, Urban Indian, or California Indian eligible for Indian Health Service — NEW under OBBBA (verification pending final FNS guidance). ELIMINATED by OBBBA (no longer exemptions): veterans, people experiencing homelessness, and former foster youth. AGE 60-64 IS A COMMON TANGLE — three answers at once: a person 60-64 is still 'elderly' (60+) for the uncapped medical and excess-shelter deductions and the LIHEAP-based utility allowance, IS exempt from the general work requirement, and cannot be forced into E&T (participation is voluntary), BUT is STILL subject to the ABAWD time limit (which now runs through 64). So a childless 60-64-year-old still needs a separate exemption (disability/unfit, a child under 14, an Indian exception, or a waived county) to avoid the 3-month limit. Being 'on Social Security' is NOT by itself an exemption: SSI or SSDI signals the disability/unfit exemption, but Social Security RETIREMENT or SURVIVOR benefits alone do not. COUNTABLE MONTHS: a month counts only if the person received a full month of benefits while not exempt, not meeting the work rule, and not in a waived area. NON-countable: a prorated/partial month, any month in which an exemption applied during ANY part of the month, good cause (illness, household emergency, lack of transportation, disaster, discrimination claim, unpredictable last-minute work hours), and discretionary exemptions. CALIFORNIA CLOCK — CRITICAL: California uses a FIXED statewide 36-month period, and the period that ran 2023-01-01 through 2025-12-31 HAS ENDED. Countable months from that period do NOT carry into the new one, so a person who 'used their 3 months' before 2026 starts fresh. Confirm the current period's exact dates against the operative CDSS ACL. REGAINING ELIGIBILITY: a person regains by working 30 consecutive days, becoming exempt, moving to a waived area, or the 36-month period ending; regaining is unlimited but requires a new application. CALIFORNIA timing: statewide ABAWD screening BEGINS 2026-06-01 (per CDSS ACL 25-93) — this is the operative date, NOT the 2025-07-04 federal signing; the prior statewide waiver expired 2026-01-31 and only a few counties still hold a waiver, so confirm the specific county. Required forms: CF 886 (CalFresh Notice of Work Rules — a verbal explanation AND the written notice must be given before the time limit is applied) and CF 377.11E (ABAWD exemption screening). Two OPTIONAL CDSS forms (released by ACL 25-34) help document the work rules: the CF 887 (CalFresh Medical Certification, for the physically/mentally-unfit exemption) and the CF 888 (ABAWD Volunteer Work Hours Verification, for community-service/volunteer hours counted toward the 80-hour rule). Some specifics (tribal-exemption and child-under-14 verification) remain pending FNS guidance — treat them as pending, not settled. Confirm the current FNS ABAWD memo, CDSS ACL, and the county waiver status for any individual case.

supplements.citation: 7 CFR 273.2(f) — verification limits; CDSS MPP 63-300, ACL 20-48 / 20-135 / 21-24 / 26-11, ACIN I-45-11
supplements.heading: Verification limits — do not over-verify
supplements.text: The single most common documented CalFresh error (CDSS Management Evaluation reviews, 2024-2025, present in 37 of 38 counties) is OVER-VERIFICATION: requesting verification the household already provided, or that is not required and not questionable. Rules: verify only what is REQUIRED (income, ineligible-noncitizen status, disability claimed for a deduction, and the other mandatory items) OR what is QUESTIONABLE — inconsistent with other statements or known facts — and when you treat something as questionable the case record must document WHY (7 CFR 273.2(f)(1)-(2) and 273.2(f)(6); California MPP 63-300.5(j), ACL 20-48, ACL 21-24, ACIN I-45-11). Do not limit the household to ONE type of verification when several would do (ACL 21-24; ACIN I-45-11), and request only the last 30 days of income (7 CFR 273.10(c)(1)(ii); ACL 20-48). Use data already available BEFORE asking the household — e.g. check The Work Number (TWN) for employer-reported wages before requesting pay stubs — but TWN data must be CONFIRMED WITH THE HOUSEHOLD before it is used to budget, and TWN should not be pulled when the household has supplied no income information at all (ACL 23-53). California also offers Truv (ACL 26-11), an optional CONSENT-BASED income, employment and work-hours verification tool that pulls this data with the client's consent and reduces manual document collection — use available data before asking the household to gather paperwork. Never re-request a document already in the case file, and never deny for 'failure to provide' verification the household in fact provided. DEDUCTIBLE-EXPENSE COROLLARY (high value, often missed): if a household does not verify a DEDUCTIBLE expense — for example shelter or utility costs — the county must determine the household's benefits WITHOUT that deduction; it may NOT deny or terminate the case for that reason (7 CFR 273.12(a)(4)(v); a repeated CDSS Management-Evaluation finding, e.g. Monterey County). Closing a case over an unverified deduction is a procedural error and a fair-hearing issue — an eligible household loses benefits it should still receive at a lower amount. Give the household a written request (CW 2200) and a minimum of 10 calendar days to respond (7 CFR 273.2(f)(5)); do not hold up an expedited-service household for non-required verification (273.2(i); ACL 16-14). Over-verification both inflates the payment/procedural error rate and wrongly denies eligible households — verify for correctness, not for volume.

supplements.citation: CF 886 (CalFresh Notice of Work Rules, rev. 8/25); CDSS ACL 22-74
supplements.heading: CF 886 — what the work-rules notice actually says
supplements.text: The CF 886 is the CalFresh Notice of Work Rules. It is INFORMATIONAL, not a sanction: it opens 'This letter is to tell you about the CalFresh work rules. If you don't follow these rules, your household's CalFresh benefits may decrease or stop.' It is issued to ALL household members — including exempt ones — at application, at recertification, and whenever a work requirement is newly imposed, and the county must ALSO give a verbal explanation (ACL 22-74). Receiving it does not mean the person is out of compliance. HOW TO READ IT: it has TWO sections with fill-in-the-blank personalization. Section 1 = the general work rules (work registration, ages 16-59); Section 2 = the ABAWD time limit. Each section has its OWN excused line, and the section qualifier matters — being excused from one does not excuse the other. Section 1 reads '____, you are excused from the general work rules because you are ____'; Section 2 reads '____, you are excused from ABAWD work requirement because you are ____'. The person's own name may appear on an excused line, so read the blanks before assuming anything. Section 2 opens with a bold 'IMPORTANT:' paragraph on the county waiver: 'You are living in a county where the ABAWD work requirement is waived. This means you do not have to meet the ABAWD work requirement at this time. We will let you know when the waiver ends.' — followed by 'When the waiver ends, you must follow the rules below:'. NOTE: that paragraph is PRE-PRINTED template text on the blank form, not a county-checked box, so its presence on a notice does NOT by itself prove the household's county is waived — confirm waiver status against the operative CDSS ACL. CONSEQUENCES: for the general work rules the disqualification ladder is 1st failure = 1 month, 2nd = 3 months, 3rd = 6 months; someone excused because they work 30+ hours/week must not voluntarily quit or reduce hours. For Section 2, ABAWDs not working or excused can get CalFresh for only 3 months in the period the county fills in. REPORTING within 10 days: income over the IRT, substantial lottery/gambling winnings, and work hours dropping below 20/week or 80/month. GOOD REASON is invited on the form itself: 'Good reasons include things out of your control like illness, no childcare for a child younger than age 12, or work conditions that are unreasonable' — and 'If the county determines that you have a good reason, there will be no change to your CalFresh benefits.' The CF 886 is a Required Form, No Substitute Permitted, and the verbal plus written notice must be given BEFORE the time limit is applied — a CF 886 that was never issued is a real procedural defense. The companion screening form is the CF 377.11E.

supplements.citation: FNS Handbook 310 (QC Review Handbook) — element codes; 7 CFR 275.12
supplements.heading: QC error element codes — what the number means
supplements.text: Federal quality control codes each finding to an ELEMENT number (the FNS-380 taxonomy in FNS Handbook 310). Non-financial: 110 age, 111 student status, 130 citizenship/non-citizen status, 140 residency, 150 household composition, 151 recipient disqualification, 160 employment & training, 161 time-limited participation (the ABAWD clock), 162 work registration, 163 voluntary quit, 164 workfare, 165 employment status, 166 acceptance of employment, 170 SSN. Resources: the 200-299 band (222 vehicles, 225 combined resources). Earned income (FNS 310 ch. 10): 311 wages and salaries, 312 self-employment, 314 other earned income. Unearned income: 331 RSDI, 332 veterans benefits, 333 SSI, 334 unemployment compensation, 335 workers' compensation, 342-347 other unearned, 350 child support received. Deductions (ch. 11) — §1100 enumerates SIX allowable deductions: 321 earned-income deduction (§1120), 323 dependent care (§1130), 361 standard deduction, 363 shelter, 365 medical, and 366 legally-obligated child support; 364 is the standard utility allowance used within the shelter calculation. Note that 321 and 323 are DEDUCTION elements, not income elements — a 323 finding turns on dependent-care expense documentation (the amount billed by a provider who is not a household member, and the name of each dependent), not on earnings, even though the deduction requires a work, training, or education nexus. In California's FY2023 QC data the largest error elements were 363 shelter and 311 wages, together about 61% of errored cases — which is why those two are where a pre-submission check pays off most. Note the element identifies WHERE the error was found, not who caused it; the separate agency/client responsibility coding answers that.

supplements.heading: When a denial or termination is procedurally invalid
supplements.text: Federal QC reviews a SAMPLE of negative actions (denials, terminations, suspensions) — not every one. §1310 draws from a negative sample frame, and §1332 excludes whole categories from review entirely: withdrawn applications, households with a pending IPV, duplicate or administrative actions, disaster denials, later months of a multi-month suspension, and closures where the household simply never reapplied at the end of its certification period. A negative action that IS reviewed is coded valid only if it: rests on a correct reason; is documented in the case record — 'when the case record does not include documentation for the specific negative action under review, the action must be coded as invalid'; is communicated in easily understandable language, meaning the reasons 'clearly describe the situation so the household is able to clearly understand why the negative action has been taken'; is procedurally correct, with every prerequisite step actually taken; and is noticed timely. IMPORTANT SCOPE NOTE: FNS Handbook 310 does NOT impose a preferred-LANGUAGE-of-issuance requirement — 'easily understandable' is about the clarity of the content, not the language it is written in. The rule that a notice must go out in the household's preferred written language is CALIFORNIA law (MPP 21-115.2; MPP 63-202.21) — cite the MPP for that, never the federal handbook, and do not tell a household that an English-only notice is federally invalid. THE RULE THAT DECIDES MOST DISPUTES: if a notice lists MULTIPLE reasons, ALL of them must be accurate — a single wrong reason invalidates the whole action (§1350.2). So a denial notice that names a reason contradicted by the case record, or two notices for the same action giving different reasons, does not stand. Specific to missed interviews: a Notice of Missed Interview is REQUIRED before any negative action based on a missed interview (§1320), a NOMI issued AFTER the denial is invalid, and the county must have attempted contact at the number in the file and documented that attempt. For a caseworker: check the reason against the record before the notice goes out. For an applicant: these are the grounds a fair hearing turns on — and if a required notice was never sent at all, the appeal clock has not started.

supplements.citation: 7 CFR 273.1 (household composition); 7 CFR 273.5 (students); CDSS ACL 24-31 (CalFresh Student Eligibility Handbook)
supplements.heading: Who counts as your SNAP household — and when you can apply separately
supplements.text: A SNAP (CalFresh) household is the people who LIVE together AND customarily BUY and PREPARE their meals together (7 CFR 273.1(a)). Living with someone does NOT by itself put you on one case — roommates, or an adult child and their parents, who shop and cook separately are SEPARATE households. THREE groups MUST be one household even if they buy and prepare food separately (7 CFR 273.1(b)): (1) spouses who live together; (2) a parent living with their own child UNDER 22 (even if that child has a spouse or children of their own); (3) a child under 18 under the parental control of an adult in the household. PRACTICAL ANSWERS people ask for: an adult 22 OR OLDER living with their parents CAN be a separate household if they buy and prepare meals separately (so a 24-year-old living with a parent who is on SSI can apply on their own); an under-22 child living with a parent CANNOT be separated out. A spouse you no longer LIVE with is not in your household — a separated (not-yet-divorced) spouse's income is not counted if you do not live together and do not buy or prepare food together; it is living-together plus shared food that decides it, not the marriage certificate. Roommates and most people sharing a dorm or apartment who do not share food are SEPARATE households — you provide information only for YOUR OWN household, not theirs. (A person who lives in your household but is not applying is a 'non-applicant': they do not have to give a Social Security Number, though their income may still be counted.) ELDERLY / DISABLED SEPARATE-HOUSEHOLD RULE: a person 60 or older who cannot buy and prepare their own meals because of a permanent disability may be a separate household from those they live with, as long as the others' income is under 165% of the federal poverty level (7 CFR 273.1(b)(2)) — a useful path for a disabled senior living with relatives. STUDENTS: a college student enrolled at least half-time in higher education is subject to special rules and is generally INELIGIBLE unless they meet a student exemption (working an average of 20 hours a week, federal or state work-study, caring for a young child, or an approved employment program) (7 CFR 273.5). California's CalFresh Student Eligibility Handbook (CDSS ACL 24-31) details these exemptions, several of which can be verified by the applicant's own statement rather than documents. Household size drives both eligibility and the benefit amount and is a top QC error element (150), so answer by who BUYS AND PREPARES FOOD together, not merely who lives at the address; confirm any close call with the county.

supplements.citation: 7 CFR 273.10(a) (initial-month proration); 7 CFR 273.2(g) and 273.2(i) (30-day and expedited standards); 7 CFR 273.17 (restored benefits)
supplements.heading: Why your first month is prorated — and why the amount changes
supplements.text: FIRST (INITIAL) MONTH IS PRORATED: benefits for the month you apply are counted from the DATE OF APPLICATION, not the whole month (7 CFR 273.10(a)(1)(ii)). Apply on the 2nd and you receive most of the month; apply on the 20th and you receive about a third. This is normal, not an error, and you do NOT get benefits for months BEFORE you applied (there is no back-pay for a gap before the application date). BUT the county has 30 days to process a normal application (7 CFR 273.2(g)) and 7 days for expedited service (7 CFR 273.2(i)); if approval comes LATE, benefits are still owed back to your APPLICATION date — a prorated first month PLUS each full month since — not merely from the approval date. A common complaint fits this exactly: applied June 2, approved July 21, but only July was paid — the household is generally owed the prorated June amount as well, and benefits lost to agency delay or error are RESTORED, up to 12 months back (7 CFR 273.17); that is an underpayment to raise with the county or on appeal. WHY THE AMOUNT CHANGES WHEN INCOME DID NOT: the benefit is computed from net income AFTER deductions, so it can swing when a DEDUCTION changes even if earnings did not. The most common cause of a sudden drop is a lost deduction — the shelter deduction, the standard utility allowance (SUA), or a medical or dependent-care deduction — frequently dropped because a verification lapsed at recertification, then restored the next period, which produces the classic 'normal, then very low, then back to normal' pattern. Other causes: income averaged or annualized differently, a change in household size, or the annual October cost-of-living adjustment. IF THE AMOUNT DROPPED SHARPLY WITH NO REAL CHANGE, ask the county WHICH deduction changed and why — an expense dropped only because it was not verified should have been budgeted, not zeroed out (see the verification-limits guidance), and the household can request a correction and a fair hearing. Do not quote a specific dollar amount or grant figure; explain the mechanism and send the person to the county for their exact numbers.

supplements.citation: 7 CFR 273.9(d)(6) (standard utility allowance) — as amended by OBBBA §10103 and §10104 (Pub. L. 119-21); CDSS ACL 25-68 (CalFresh SUAs / State Utility Assistance Subsidy)
supplements.heading: Utility allowance (SUA), LIHEAP and internet — what OBBBA changed
supplements.text: The Standard Utility Allowance (SUA) is a fixed utility figure used inside the excess-shelter deduction; the largest is the Heating and Cooling SUA (HCSUA), and qualifying for it RAISES the benefit. LIHEAP / ENERGY-ASSISTANCE CHANGE (OBBBA §10103, effective 7/4/2025): receiving a LIHEAP (or similar energy-assistance) payment now automatically confers the HCSUA ONLY for a household that includes an ELDERLY (age 60 or older) or DISABLED member. A household with NO elderly or disabled member no longer gets the HCSUA automatically from a LIHEAP payment — BUT it can still get the HCSUA the ordinary way, by actually INCURRING heating or cooling costs, so those households should report their utility costs at recertification. Nothing changed for elderly/disabled households. LOOKBACK: for an elderly/disabled household a qualifying energy-assistance payment counts if it was received in the month of application OR in the prior 12 months — an older payment still helps. WEATHERIZATION: a weatherization payment counts as 'other similar energy assistance,' so the same elderly/disabled condition applies to it for the HCSUA; but a ONE-TIME weatherization or emergency energy repair/replacement payment is NOT counted as income at all — two separate rules, so do not conflate 'does it give the HCSUA' with 'is it income.' MID-CERTIFICATION PROTECTION: a State may NOT strip the HCSUA from an ONGOING non-elderly/non-disabled household in the middle of its certification period, cannot send a request-for-contact just for that, and cannot close the case for non-response — the change is applied at the next RECERTIFICATION, not immediately. SPLIT HOUSEHOLD: if a household with an elderly/disabled member splits into two SNAP households, each new household is tested SEPARATELY for an elderly/disabled member; a split-off household without one falls back to the incur-costs test. INTERNET (OBBBA §10104, effective 7/4/2025): internet, broadband or Wi-Fi costs may NO LONGER be counted in the excess-shelter deduction or in any SUA — do not advise reporting internet to raise the benefit. Internet itself can never be counted; if it is bundled with other, genuinely allowable utilities on one bill, the internet portion is excluded and the county determines how the rest of the bill is treated — have the household ask the county about a combined bill rather than assuming a split. IMPORTANT FRAMING: every rule here changes the benefit AMOUNT, not whether the household QUALIFIES — never tell someone they are ineligible over a utility or internet issue, and never quote a specific SUA dollar figure. In California the heating/cooling allowance is conferred through the State Utility Assistance Subsidy (SUAS), whose eligibility criteria OBBBA changed and CDSS implemented in ACL 25-68; the state sets its SUA values statewide, so send the person to the county or CDSS for the current amounts.

supplements.citation: OBBBA §10108 (Pub. L. 119-21); 7 CFR 273.4 (alien eligibility); PRWORA 5-year bar — PROVISIONAL, under active litigation (NY v. Rollins)
supplements.heading: Noncitizen SNAP eligibility (§10108) — PROVISIONAL, confirm with a caseworker or legal aid
supplements.text: IMPORTANT — this area changed on 7/4/2025 (OBBBA §10108) AND is under active litigation (New York v. Rollins, in which California is a plaintiff), so enforcement in California is in flux. NEVER give a definitive yes/no on immigration-based eligibility; explain the general rule and route the person to their county caseworker AND a nonprofit immigration legal-aid provider for a determination on their own facts. GENERAL RULE post-7/4/2025: the immigration statuses that confer SNAP eligibility BY STATUS were narrowed to LAWFUL PERMANENT RESIDENT (green card), CUBAN/HAITIAN ENTRANT, and COFA (Freely Associated States) citizen. Refugees and asylees — including children under 18 — are no longer eligible by that status ALONE. Two things soften this and MUST be surfaced so no one wrongly self-excludes: (1) a former refugee, asylee, or trafficking survivor who has SINCE ADJUSTED to LPR (has a green card now) IS eligible, and is NOT required to serve a new 5-year wait — so always ask 'do you have a green card now?' before saying no; (2) the 5-year PRWORA waiting period for LPRs is UNCHANGED by OBBBA, and is waived for anyone under 18, blind/disabled, with 40 qualifying work quarters, a U.S. military connection, or who adjusted from a wait-exempt status. MIXED-STATUS HOUSEHOLDS (counter the chilling effect): if some members are ineligible, the ELIGIBLE members — especially U.S.-citizen or LPR children — can STILL receive SNAP. The ineligible member is a 'non-applicant': they do not have to give an SSN or immigration status, though their income may still be counted (in full or pro-rated). Applying for the eligible members does not force the ineligible member to disclose status. CALIFORNIA FALLBACK: many immigrants excluded from federal SNAP may qualify for the California Food Assistance Program (CFAP), the state-funded analog — refer them there instead of a dead end. PUBLIC CHARGE: SNAP is generally not counted for most family members for public-charge purposes, but that is a legal question — do not give a conclusion; send it to immigration legal aid. Always confirm the current litigation status (NY v. Rollins) and current CDSS guidance before stating any of this as settled.

supersessions.273.24: (California: statewide time limits resumed 2026-06-01 per CDSS ACL 25-93; only a few counties hold a waiver — confirm the specific county.)
